extracted.intended_audience: scientifically literate general readers and students of geology/earth science (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used to judge hypotheses about the Earth's interior, volcanism, earthquakes, and cosmogony (e.g., liquid vs solid nucleus, role of water, tidal effects). Focuses on how observational, experimental, and theoretical evidence support or refute competing models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the agency of water in volcanic phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence and action of water (especially sea-water) must be incorporated in explanations of volcanic activity: vapors are principal constituents of eruptions and can be generated by infiltration of sea-water into subterranean reservoirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited: M. Fouque's estimates of vapor volume from Etna (1865); chemical analyses showing marine salt and decomposition products in fumaroles and emanations from Vesuvius, Etna, Santorin. Mechanistic guidance: seawater percolates via fissures or transudation, vaporizes on contact with incandescent lava, and accumulated steam can cause explosive eruptions; vapors increase lava fluidity and may cause secondary explosions as vapors escape. A satisfactory theory must explain these observations and processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the enormous volumes and energy of eruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis must plausibly account for the prodigious volumes of material (lava, scoriae, pumice, ashes) emitted in eruptions and the mechanical force required to eject them to great distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Kilauea (1840) estimated at 5.5 billion m^3; Skapta-Jokull (1783) comparable to Mont Blanc (~500 billion m^3); Tomboro (1815) scoriae/ashes thrown 500 km. Theorists must provide mechanisms that produce the required energy and explain how such masses are raised and projected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match realistic temperature/depth conditions for molten material
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must be consistent with plausible temperature estimates and need not invoke extreme depths to account for molten matter; it must show how fusion and steam pressures arise at the posited depths/temperatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text estimates crater-bottom incandescent mass at ~2000°C and notes that steam pressure at temperatures above ~1200°C would be ample to explain explosive force. The crust may be thinner in volcanic regions; therefore, explanations should consider variable crustal thickness and do not require extreme central depths like 20 km for molten material to exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform to seismic/astronomical perturbation constraints (precession/nutation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Models (particularly liquid-nucleus hypotheses) must be consistent with observed precession and nutation; luni-solar perturbations place constraints on how much of the globe yields to tidal/attracting forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hopkins' calculations argued a crust thickness of 1300–1600 km to reconcile a liquid nucleus with observed precession/nutation; Sir W. Thomson's 'Memoir on the Rigidity of the Earth' supports this constraint. Any model implying a thin crust over a liquid core must show it does not produce precession/nutation rates inconsistent with observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for observed correlations between earthquakes and lunar phases/perigee/lunar day
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory theory should explain statistical periodicities in earthquake occurrence correlated with lunar phases (syzygia), perigee/apogee, and the lunar day (meridian passages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M. Perrey's compilation (125 years of observations) showed two maxima in frequency at new and full moon and minima at quarters; comparisons with perigee/apogee yielded differences favoring perigee; local studies (Arequipa, Monteleone/Messina journals, Arcovito at Reggio) also show preponderance at moon's meridian passages. Theories should incorporate mechanisms for such modulation (subterranean tides, tidal stresses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predict or allow for subterranean tide-movements (tidal modulation of lava flows)
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility of tide-like movements in subsurface molten material should be admitted and, where data exist, predictions should match observations of periodic variations in lava flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Scacchi and Palmieri observed twice-daily increases in Vesuvius lava flow (May 1855) with ~12-hour intervals and small retardation similar to ocean tides; recommendation that such observations be made at lava lakes (Kilauea). A theory ought to anticipate or explain such periodicities if subterranean masses respond to lunar/solar tides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent with material physical properties under pressure (solidification behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses about the state (solid/liquid/pasty) of the interior must respect experimental results on how materials behave under high pressure/temperature—whether they expand or contract on solidification and how pressure affects melting points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: James Thomson pointed out compression can lower the point of fusion for substances that expand on solidifying (water) and raise it for those that contract; Bischof's experiments indicate many rocks expand by fusion and contract in solidifying (granite, schists, trachyte shrink ≈1/5); Siemens observed vitreous masses showing complex contraction/expansion behavior. These experimental facts bear directly on whether a central nucleus is likely to be solid or liquid and on whether solidification would begin at surface or center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain mountain uplift and surface configuration consistently with geognosy
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen theory must provide plausible mechanisms for mountain formation, elevation episodes, and the resulting surface configuration and stratigraphy (including timing/chronology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Elie de Beaumont's internal-fire model (contraction of the crust causing fissures, lava forcing and folding edges to form ridges) vs. Lyell's uniformitarianism (slow ongoing processes). The critique targets synchronism assumptions and energy budgets (J. Bertrand's similitude arguments). The model should explain sedimentary deposition over disruptions and the apparent chronology of successive elevations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agree with astronomical/cosmogonic constraints (planetary orbital properties and spectroscopic evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosmogonic theories (e.g., Laplace's nebular hypothesis) must account for planetary orbital characteristics (low eccentricity, low inclination, common rotation/revolution direction) and be supported by spectroscopic observations of nebulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laplace's model explains the slight eccentricity/inclination and direction identity; spectroscopic analysis shows some nebulae are gaseous and display structures (rings, gyratory motion) compatible with nebular condensation and ring formation. Modern validations (Roche's analysis of equatorial ridge/ring formation) also serve as tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be grounded in laboratory/experimental verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical claims about interior processes should be tested and informed by laboratory experiments and material observations (melting/solidification behavior, viscosity effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited experiments: Bischof on rock behavior, Mallet on scoriae, Siemens' glassworks experiments, Champagneur's lab demonstrations of liquid rotation under viscous coupling. Theories should reference and be compatible with such empirical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate viscosity/frictional coupling when assessing rotational/rigidity effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments about differential rotation between crust and interior must account for the nonzero viscosity of interior liquids under enormous pressure, which leads to frictional coupling that can cause the interior to follow the crust's motion for very slow accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delaunay's critique: a viscous fluid under large pressure will likely rotate with the shell given the extremely slight accelerations involved in precession/nutation; Champagneur's experiments illustrate the effect. Therefore, any calculation assuming perfect decoupling must justify neglecting viscosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify rigidity effects on tidal amplitudes and related observables
rubrics_metrics.description: Models must use plausible rigidity values for the globe to predict tidal deformation, and reconcile these predictions with measured oceanic tides and precessional/nutation data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomson's estimate: if average rigidity comparable to glass, the globe's deformation is ~0.6 of that for a liquid; deducting this reduces tide height to ~0.4 of the rigid-ball prediction. Theories must use similar quantitative reasoning to ensure consistency with tidal observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer hypotheses supported by multiple converging lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptability of a model is strengthened by concordant evidence from diverse domains (chemical analyses, volumetric eruption data, seismic observations, astronomical calculations, laboratory experiments, spectroscopic studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly evaluates competing theories by their fit to many types of data (e.g., Fouque's chemical analyses, Perrey's seismic statistics, Roche's mechanics, spectral analysis of nebulae). Single-line explanations (purely chemical oxidation of nucleus, or unsupported cataclysmic claims) are criticized for lack of broad support.
